subject: Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
Hello,

I am going through and compiling a booklet for students of mine of things I've found useful when using Stan.

I want to create a simple example -- using fake data generated in R -- that produces divergent iterations. I know that I could use Neal's funnel example to generate such issues, but I was hoping to create a simpler (non-hierarchical) example. 

At the moment I have got an example of correlated regressors that produces some divergent iterations, but isn't quite as profound/simple-to-interpret as I'd hoped.

As such I was wondering, are there any examples that anyone has that generate divergent iterations? 

Best,

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
Try something with a multiplicative nonidentifiabiliy, as in

parameters {
  real x1;
  real x2;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model {
  y ~ normal(x1 * x2, sigma);
}

You might have to play around with the priors/simulated data
to make the tails sharp enough to throw divergences.

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
Thanks very much. The following works pretty nicely. The plot of samples of a against b shows lots of divergent iterations near zero.

In R,

a <- 2
b <- 4
sigma <- 1
N <- 10
X <- rnorm(N,a*b,sigma)
priora_1=2
priora_2=100,
priorb_1=4
priorb_2=100

In Stan,

data { 
  int N; 
  real X[N]; 
  real priora_1;
  real priora_2;
  real priorb_1;
  real priorb_2;
} 

parameters { 
  real a;
  real b;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}

model { 
  X ~ normal(a*b,sigma);
  sigma ~ lognormal(0,1);
  a ~ normal(priora_1,priora_2);
  b ~ normal(priorb_1,priorb_2);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
I'd highly recommend either (a) just hard-coding the
priors, or (b) naming them something sensible, like
mu_1 and sigma_1 and mu_2 and sigma_2. Especially if
it's going to be for students.

If you don't have any priors, it'll diverge like the additive
example in the manual because the posterior is improper.
With priors, you should get the nice banana shape posterior,
which also illustrates why a single mass matrix can't work
over all of some posteriors.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
On Sunday, August 21, 2016 at 11:31:47 AM UTC-4, Ben Lambert wrote:
I want to create a simple example -- using fake data generated in R -- that produces divergent iterations. I know that I could use Neal's funnel example to generate such issues, but I was hoping to create a simpler (non-hierarchical) example.

Depends on what constitutes simple. To me, introducing a unnecessary product or sum of two things when the data are only informative about the combination is self-inflicted. Also, data are unnecessary. You can get a lot of divergences drawing from a distribution that has two standard normal marginals and almost any copula to induce asymmetric dependence. Attached is an example with a Clayton copula. If data = list(alpha = alpha) where alpha >= 7 all the divergences are in the lower triangle of the pairs plot.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
Absolutely self-inflicted, but also simple pedagogically.
Andrew and I disagree on the same point---he wants to use realistic
examples, whereas I want to use minimal cases. I'm guessing this
is an applied-stas vs. computer-science vs. math thing.
In compute science, we love our "hello world" programs.

The lack of simple examples in BDA and R docs were a real burden
for me when I was (am in the case of R) trying to learn. And
what's simple/minimal to a (Bayesian) stats or R expert vs.
a new learner varies wildly, which is why I like to keep it
simple. The more advanced students will understand (even if
they're annoyed) and so will the beginners.

Of course, the final call here is up to Ben Lambert.

- Bob

messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Simplest example of a model that yields divergent iterations
parts:
Thanks both. I must say I prefer the computationally-straightforward example that Michael suggested. However I agree that it is difficult to think of a situation where we would actually use a model like this one. As such I have resorted to using a model that we use in mark-release-recapture experiments -- where we release N marked organisms on day 0 and monitor their recaptures. If we assume a Weibull mortality (where the mortality hazard changes with age) then we can estimate its parameters using the Stan model below. Here psi is the daily recapture prob, mu and beta are parameters of the Weibull. 

This produces significant divergent iterations -- due to the non-linear interaction of the mu and beta parameters. 

data { 
  int N; 
  int Y[N];
  int numReleased;
}

parameters { 
  real<lower=0,upper=1> psi;
  real<lower=0> mu;
  real<lower=0> beta;
}

model { 
  for(t in 1:N)
    Y[t] ~ binomial(numReleased,psi * exp(-mu*(t^beta)));
}
